# Shared proxies: audit payload ownership, not only launches

PR #238 supplied the cache-proxy design sources; my performance review was of #239, not an independent #238 review.

The reusable lesson from PERF-239-01: audit full-payload ownership across an upstream await. `Rewritten.body` was `Option<Vec<u8>>`; cloning it retained a second serialized prompt while forwarding. On a shared sidecar, that avoidable memory scales with body size times active requests. A per-request 64 MiB limit is not a fleet-wide memory bound. Destructure the rewrite, move its vector into `Bytes::from`, and keep only metadata. The retry's `Bytes::clone()` intentionally shares the payload and should remain. Inspect ownership directly: ordinary response/content tests do not prove an allocation was removed.

Req-14 reuses the existing JSON parse. Borrowed-header classification returns enums/static strings; an explicit initiator avoids inference; subagents skip the TTL walk and, without model mapping, serialization. Describe this precisely as no extra launch, network call, timer, parse or prompt-sized copy, not literally zero CPU instructions. The shape field extends an existing log record rather than adding one.

A surviving mutation is a proof limit, not automatically a new blocker. The readiness-snapshot guard remained present; performance acceptance did not clear F001 for correctness or security. C34 makes extra mutation fixtures optional.

Magic wand: extend the existing fake-upstream cost scenario with large prompts and concurrent clients, recording peak RSS and latency alongside launch counters. No new benchmark framework is needed. A response that streams and a flat process counter can still hide substantial prompt-buffer amplification.

Evidence: `crates/cache-proxy/src/proxy.rs` (body move and shared retry), `crates/cache-proxy/src/rewrite.rs` (subagent path), plan 228 `assets/evidence/live-rows.md`, and performance outputs `18-verdict-pr-239-91e7d31` / `18-verdict-pr-239-fe6811f`.
